description: Developing a public facing interface for object classification using SPHEREx artifacts.
summary: Our project transforms NASA’s SPHEREx data into an interactive, public facing observatory that makes astronomical discovery accessible to everyone, regardless of expertise. Users can enter sky coordinates to visualize how objects change over time, making it easier to identify moving objects such as asteroids, comets, and brown dwarfs. Beyond the core challenge, we expanded the tool with individual detector-band filtering, multi-band image combination, on the fly spectrum generation, and Gaia data overlays. We also introduced a collaborative discovery platform where users can flag interesting findings, share them with the community, and explore the most frequently flagged observations to surface promising discoveries. Our goal is to turn SPHEREx's massive dataset into an accessible, collaborative discovery experience that empowers anyone with an interest in astronomy to participate in scientific exploration.
details:
SCOPE (SPHEREx Citizen Observatory for Public Exploration) is a web viewer that makes NASA’s SPHEREx infrared images easy for anyone to explore. Users enter any spot in the sky, flip through every image of it across all six infrared bands and across dates, and spot objects that move. They can also combine a day’s images, overlay Gaia star positions, and pull a 102-color spectrum to see what an object is made of.

We built it in Python 3.12 using astropy, astroquery, pyvo, numpy, reproject, astropy-healpix, matplotlib and requests, with data from NASA IRSA (SPHEREx images and spectral cubes) and Gaia DR3 via MAST. It runs as a local web server with an HTML/JS front end and is deployed with Docker. SCOPE works like a blink comparator, the flip-between-photos method that found Pluto, rebuilt for a modern infrared survey, and it gets each spectrum by reading only the small slice of a ~320 MB data file it needs. Our team focused on ease of use for non-experts (a built-in guide and hover tips), fair comparisons between images (each one evened out and known bad pixels skipped), speed through caching, and accuracy, including correcting star positions for how far they’ve moved since 2016.
